segments.title: If Jellicoe had turned towards the torpedoes at Jutland
segments.body: Turning towards the torpedoes at Jutland could have cost Jellicoe about a third of his capital ships or more. The estimate is speculative and depends on how many ships were hit. It also depends on how well their underwater protection contained the damage. The outcome of the battle is left open.

evidence.note: A speculative capital-ship loss estimate depends on torpedo hits and the effectiveness of underwater protection.

segments.summary: A counterfactual about British capital-ship losses turns on the number of hits and how well the ships withstand them.
segments.question: How many capital ships might Jellicoe have lost if he had turned towards the torpedoes at Jutland, and what would that have meant for the battle?
segments.answerShort: The estimate is about a third of the capital ships or potentially more. The estimate depends on how many ships were hit and how well their underwater protection held.

segments.title: Anime mascots and military recruiting in Japan
segments.body: Anime mascots and military-themed entertainment are judged effective recruiting tools in Japan. The question includes a claim about military funding for games such as Azur Lane and anime about service life, but no funding arrangement is identified. The effectiveness of the same recruiting approach in other countries remains uncertain.

evidence.note: An affirmative assessment of anime-based recruiting in Japan. Financial support for Azur Lane and anime appears in the question's premise, without supporting details.

segments.summary: Anime mascots receive a positive assessment as recruiting tools in Japan, with uncertainty about whether other countries would achieve similar results.
segments.question: Do Japan's armed forces use anime mascots and games to help recruit, and could the same approach work elsewhere?
segments.answerShort: Yes, anime mascots and related entertainment are judged effective for recruitment in Japan. Their effectiveness elsewhere remains uncertain.

segments.title: Designing an all-calibres battleship in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The audience's challenge is to fit every available gun calibre onto one Soviet battleship hull in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts. The build starts with 20-inch, 19-inch and 18-inch weapons. As the mounts go aboard, the hull needs more beam and the design speed comes down to 28 knots. Switching the largest weapons to triple turrets creates more room for the remaining calibres. The remaining 8-inch mount is fitted at the end of the exercise.

evidence.note: Soviet hull selection, the largest gun calibres, increased beam, a 28-knot speed setting and triple turrets chosen to save space.
The brief is clarified as one gun of every calibre, and the remaining 8-inch mount is fitted.

segments.summary: An audience challenge to fit every available calibre onto a Soviet hull puts beam, speed and turret arrangement in competition.
segments.question: Can one battleship carry a gun of every available calibre in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts?
segments.answerShort: Yes. The game build uses a Soviet battleship hull, adds beam, reduces speed to 28 knots and uses triple turrets for its largest guns to make room for the full range of calibres.

segments.title: The all-calibres battleship's crowded battery and fire-control problem
segments.body: The mixed battery is already expected to be a fire-control nightmare while smaller weapons are still going aboard. Single 13-inch and 12-inch mounts are fitted before the work moves down through 11-inch, 10-inch and 9-inch guns to the secondaries. The turrets require individual placement wherever deck space remains. Finding room for each mount leaves the separate problem of coordinating fire from all these weapons.

evidence.note: Explicit warning about fire control, followed by the fitting of individual heavy-gun mounts before work begins on the secondaries.

segments.summary: The all-calibres game battleship has a crowded deck plan and a battery expected to be difficult to control.

segments.title: Gun placement, stability and engine efficiency
segments.body: Spaces around the funnels and towards the ends of the ship appear to offer room for more guns. The proposed positions change the game's stability profile and engine-efficiency rating. Stability is already a problem on the all-calibres battleship. Leaving some apparent mounting space unused is therefore an attempt to make the design more manageable.

evidence.note: The suggested gun positions are rejected because of their effects on the game's stability and engine-efficiency values.

segments.summary: A suggestion to use spaces around the funnel or at the ends of the ship exposes the compromises in a crowded battleship design.
segments.question: Why avoid placing guns near the funnels or at the ends of the all-calibres game battleship?
segments.answerShort: The proposed positions affect the game's stability and engine-efficiency ratings on a ship whose stability is already a concern.

segments.title: Keeping the all-calibres battleship usable in the game
segments.body: Ranging equipment, hydrophones and radio join the all-calibres battleship's armament. Veteran crew settings are chosen to give the unusual battery a chance in action. Turbine machinery, maximum bulkheads, a double hull and torpedo defences complete the supporting fit. Even with these aids, controlling so many different guns is expected to remain difficult.

evidence.note: Ranging equipment, acoustic detection, radio, veteran crew settings and protective arrangements are selected for the mixed-calibre game ship.

segments.summary: After the guns go aboard, the design adds ranging equipment, radio and protection for a ship expected to be hard to fight.

segments.title: Speed and space in a simulated British battleship
segments.body: Even a game hull described as displacing 112,000 tons runs up against the designer's limits. Reducing its speed to 28 knots releases space, and further reductions open room for range and equipment. Spacious crew accommodation takes part of that allowance. A proposed 16.5-inch gun fit then gives way to further armament trials when it proves difficult to place on the hull.

evidence.note: A 112,000-ton hull gains design capacity when its speed is reduced to 28 knots, followed by accommodation and gun-fit adjustments.

segments.summary: Reducing the speed requirement opens room for armament and crew accommodations in the Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts designer.

segments.title: A Town-class cruiser's worth of guns on each side
segments.body: Six-inch secondary guns give the game battleship something like a Town-class cruiser's battery on each side. Quintuple launchers with 23-inch torpedoes add underwater armament. Super-heavy shells are selected, and ammunition and firing-rate settings are adjusted before the trial. The proposed British opponent therefore carries a substantial secondary battery alongside its main guns.

evidence.note: The 6-inch batteries are compared with a Town-class cruiser on each beam, followed by quintuple torpedo mounts and a 23-inch torpedo setting.

segments.summary: A British game battleship carries a secondary battery compared to a Town-class cruiser's armament on either beam.

segments.title: Armour, pitch and trim on the simulated Duncan
segments.body: The design work turns from weapons to the main deck, belt armour and stability. Reducing pitch and roll is meant to give the guns a steadier platform. Changes to the main belt and fore-and-aft weight bring the hull closer to balance. Some stern-heavy trim remains when the design is renamed Duncan.

evidence.note: Deck and belt adjustments, efforts to reduce pitch and roll, persistent stern-heavy trim and the choice of Duncan as the game ship's name.

segments.summary: The British design is adjusted for steadier gunnery while its armour and fore-and-aft balance are still being worked out.

segments.title: Radar and ranging with a mixed-calibre battery
segments.body: Before launch, the Soviet design receives a check of its auxiliary machinery and stability. The aim is to give its unusual battery a steadier firing platform. Radar is thought to help once the ships are in action. Ranging the shots from so many different weapons remains a problem despite that assistance.

evidence.note: Pre-launch machinery and stability checks, followed by a qualified assessment of radar assistance and an explicit warning about ranging the mixed battery.

segments.summary: Radar may assist the Soviet game battleship, but ranging shots from its many different guns remains a serious difficulty.

segments.title: Scaling a King George V design to 18-inch guns
segments.body: Duncan adapts a twelve-gun King George V scheme to an 18-inch main battery in the game. The opposing mixed-calibre ship is struggling to score hits despite efforts to give it a stable platform. The trial contrasts that assortment of weapons with Duncan's concentrated heavy battery. The mixed-calibre ship sinks.

evidence.note: Duncan's twelve 18-inch guns derive from a scaled-up King George V scheme, while the opposing ship struggles to hit and sinks.

segments.summary: A twelve-gun King George V scheme supplies the starting point for the British game ship Duncan.

segments.title: British awareness of Japan's Number 13 class
segments.body: Britain had some awareness of Japan's plans for the Number 13 class. The extent and detail of that knowledge remain unspecified.

evidence.note: Affirmative answer to whether Britain knew about the Number 13 class, without further intelligence details.

segments.summary: Britain had some awareness of Japan's prospective Number 13 battleships, although the extent of its knowledge is left unspecified.
segments.question: Did Britain know about Japan's Number 13 class?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Britain had some idea of what Japan was planning.

segments.title: Why battlecruisers could struggle to stay in a battle line
segments.body: Battlecruisers could form a line, but their reliance on speed and manoeuvre could break up the formation during combat. In this tactical interpretation, sharp changes of course help protect a battlecruiser, while a battleship can rely more heavily on armour. Combining the two creates a difficult choice. A battleship struggling to follow the faster ship's manoeuvres can compromise its gunnery. A battlecruiser held to the battleship's steadier profile loses some of the freedom of movement on which its survival depends.

evidence.note: Different manoeuvring profiles create a choice between impaired battleship gunnery and restricted battlecruiser movement.

segments.summary: Speed and freedom to manoeuvre help explain why a line of battlecruisers could break up once the fighting started.
segments.question: Would battlecruisers use the same line-of-battle tactics as battleships when fighting other battlecruisers?
segments.answerShort: They could form a line. The need to keep speed up and manoeuvre freely could soon break that formation.

segments.title: Can a 40-knot battlecruiser carry 15-inch guns and armour?
segments.body: The brief calls for 40 knots, guns of at least 15 inches and some armour. Gas turbines, hull adjustments and reductions in protection bring the design within the game's displacement allowance. Its twelve 15-inch guns sit forward to balance the hull. The stated cruising speed is 33 knots, separate from the 40-knot design target. A heavy cruiser is chosen as the sort of opponent a lone battlecruiser might hunt, and the completed ship withstands a torpedo hit during the trial.

evidence.note: The 40-knot requirement leads to a gas-turbine design with twelve forward 15-inch guns, reduced armour and survival of a simulated torpedo hit.

segments.summary: The game challenge produces a long, slim battlecruiser with all twelve main guns forward for a trial against a heavy cruiser.
segments.question: Can you build a 40-knot battlecruiser with 15-inch guns and some armour?
segments.answerShort: The simulator allows a 40-knot design with twelve 15-inch guns and some armour after changes to hull dimensions, propulsion and weight.

segments.title: Hull and machinery for a 40-knot game battlecruiser
segments.body: A heavy cruiser is chosen as the opponent before work begins on the 40-knot hull. Several hulls look plausible in the designer, and the selected one needs a little more beam. The available fittings rule out the enhanced options being tried. At least one funnel must fit, and range is reduced to about 24,000 kilometres before attention turns to the 15-inch guns.

evidence.note: Hull selection, increased beam, restricted fittings and a roughly 24,000-kilometre range precede fitting the main battery.

segments.summary: The requested speed drives the choice of hull, beam and the machinery fittings that will fit aboard.

segments.title: Paying for 40 knots in armour and displacement
segments.body: The design starts with the desired capabilities and pares them back against the game's displacement limit. Twelve main guns set the baseline, while hull protection and bulkheads offer places to reduce weight. Gas turbines provide the 40-knot target after diesel propulsion is rejected. The ship remains overweight before the armour adjustments. Progressive armour cuts bring it under the limit and release some weight for secondary guns.

evidence.note: Gas turbines meet the speed target, then reductions in protection bring the twelve-gun design within its displacement allowance.

segments.summary: Once the speed and main battery are set, hull protection has to fit the remaining weight.

segments.title: Radar, secondary guns and exposed armour on the 40-knot design
segments.body: Twin 5.5-inch secondary guns add weight to a design already close to its limit. Radar is retained when the ship comes out roughly 500 tons overweight. Armour is reduced selectively, with thicker protection kept on the exposed upper area expected to draw fire. Further adjustments bring the ship back within its allowance.

evidence.note: Twin 5.5-inch guns and retained radar require selective armour cuts, while an exposed upper area keeps thicker protection.

segments.summary: The last weight cuts preserve radar and concentrate armour on the parts expected to be exposed to fire.

segments.title: Twelve guns forward on the simulated battlecruiser
segments.body: The simulated battlecruiser has a long, slim hull and a stated cruising speed of 33 knots. Its twelve 15-inch guns sit forward to balance the fore-and-aft weight distribution. The unusual arrangement therefore serves a specific purpose in the game's design model. During the engagement with the heavy cruiser, the battlecruiser withstands a torpedo hit.

evidence.note: Forward placement of twelve 15-inch guns is justified by weight balance, and the ship survives a torpedo hit in the trial.

segments.summary: The finished hull puts the main battery forward to balance its weight and takes a torpedo hit during the trial.

segments.title: Optically guided weapons versus heavy naval guns
segments.body: Optically guided ship-to-ship weapons had been contemplated. For the application proposed here, usable guidance would put the firing ship within heavy-gun range. Heavy guns were judged more efficient at those engagement distances, which undermined the case for the guided weapon.

evidence.note: The proposed optical-guidance range overlaps heavy-gun range, where guns are judged more efficient.

segments.summary: Optical guidance offered little advantage in the proposed engagement because heavy naval guns could already reach the target.
segments.question: Were optically guided ship-to-ship weapons contemplated, and were they practical?
segments.answerShort: They were contemplated. At the ranges envisaged, heavy naval guns could already engage the target more efficiently.

segments.title: A post-1920 ship with its firepower on the beams
segments.body: The brief allows any nation and calls for a ship from after 1920. Most of its firepower must face outward from rows along the sides, with restricted arcs. The resulting game cruiser masses 6-inch guns and must turn beam-on to use them in its trial. It fulfils the broadside concept but only partially matches the original layout restrictions.

evidence.note: Post-1920 design challenge specifying outward-facing rows of weapons and restricted arcs.
The cruiser turns beam-on to fire its massed 6-inch battery during the simulated engagement.
Acknowledgement that the completed broadside ship only partially followed the requested layout.

segments.summary: A game build translates rows of outward-facing guns into a broadside cruiser with restricted firing arcs.
segments.question: Can you build a post-1920 ship carrying most of its firepower in outward-facing rows along its sides?
segments.answerShort: The game produces a cruiser with rows of 6-inch guns for fighting beam-on. It only partially matches the brief.

segments.title: Fitting a broadside battery into a 20,000-ton cruiser
segments.body: The simulated cruiser reaches about 20,000 tons. Its 6-inch and smaller guns initially have wider arcs than the brief allows, so their coverage is deliberately restricted. Triple torpedo mounts are added, and the ship ends up roughly 600 tons overweight. Switching to a double hull saves about 300 tons, leaving further weight to remove before the trial.

evidence.note: Restricted firing arcs, triple torpedo mounts and a roughly 600-ton excess lead to a double-hull substitution and further weight cuts.

segments.summary: The broadside design narrows gun arcs and trades hull protection against the weight of additional weapons.

segments.title: A massed 6-inch broadside against heavier guns
segments.body: The broadside ship has to turn beam-on to bring its rows of guns to bear. The volume of 6-inch fire prompts a distinction between armour surviving an initial strike and enduring repeated impacts. The simulated ship carries the lighter battery on a heavy-cruiser-sized hull. The fight is close enough for a mutual loss to look plausible before it ends.

evidence.note: Beam-on firing brings the 6-inch battery to bear, with repeated hits testing armour after it stops initial impacts.

segments.summary: A game cruiser has to expose its side to use the full weight of its lighter guns against a heavy cruiser.

segments.title: What holding Singapore would have required in World War II
segments.body: An armoured division and at least one more infantry division are proposed to counter Japanese manoeuvre in Malaya. The fleet would have had at least four carriers and four capital ships, backed by escorts, submarines and supply ships. The local air force would probably have needed to be trebled. Even if that concentration made defence possible, assigning those resources to Singapore would have left other fronts short.

evidence.note: Proposed reinforcement includes an armoured division, another infantry division, four carriers, four capital ships, supporting vessels and a trebled air force, at the expense of other fronts.

segments.summary: A counterfactual weighs the land, air and naval reinforcements needed in Malaya against the demands of other fronts.
segments.question: What would it have taken to hold Singapore during World War II?
segments.answerShort: Major land and air reinforcements and a large, supported fleet would have been needed at the cost of forces on other fronts.

segments.title: A battleship with battlecruiser armour
segments.body: The game challenge reduces a battleship's protection towards battlecruiser levels while retaining twelve 18-inch guns. A 6-inch belt is attempted, although the simulator prevents one armour setting from going below 7 inches. The Russian heavy cruiser begins astern in fog and is quickly overwhelmed by the heavy battery. Roughly three 18-inch hits are enough in this encounter. That result tests the battleship's offensive power more clearly than its reduced protection.

evidence.note: Attempted reduction to a 6-inch belt encounters a 7-inch minimum on an unspecified armour setting, followed by a short fight decided by the battleship's 18-inch guns.

segments.summary: A viewer's design challenge puts a lightly protected battleship with twelve 18-inch guns against a Russian heavy cruiser in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.
segments.question: Can you build a battleship with battlecruiser-style armour?
segments.answerShort: The game build reduces its armour and retains twelve 18-inch guns, which quickly overwhelm the heavy cruiser used for the trial.

segments.title: A 1938 Tribal-class successor in the game
segments.body: The game design takes shape around a 1938 fit with torpedoes and 4.5-inch guns. A 40-calibre barrel is preferred for the 4.5-inch gun, and the simulator offers a shorter weapon. The design speed comes down to 36 knots. The available curved towers are judged unlike Royal Navy practice of the period. The design is called Trafalgar and still has stability problems.

evidence.note: Tribal-successor prompt leads to a 1938 design called Trafalgar, with 4.5-inch guns, torpedoes and a reduced speed of 36 knots.

segments.summary: A 1938-era design in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts explores what a successor to the Royal Navy's Tribal class could carry.
segments.question: What would a replacement for the Tribal-class destroyer look like?
segments.answerShort: The proposed game design uses a 1938 setting, torpedoes and 4.5-inch guns at 36 knots, but its available fittings and stability still need adjustment.

segments.title: Royal Navy torpedo options beyond the standard calibre
segments.body: The simulated destroyer's 23-inch torpedo fit raises a distinction between a standard weapon and an available development option. British work on a larger torpedo is the justification for retaining it. In this counterfactual, an option that had not been pushed forward becomes available to the designer. The historical calibre and associated class remain uncertain in the captions.

evidence.note: Challenge to a 23-inch fit receives a development-history justification, but the associated class name is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: British torpedo development provides the proposed justification for a nonstandard fit on the counterfactual destroyer.
segments.question: Why use a nonstandard torpedo calibre on the British destroyer design?
segments.answerShort: Earlier British development work makes the larger torpedo a proposed counterfactual option, although the historical designation is unclear.

segments.title: Pitch and weight distribution on a destroyer design
segments.body: The proposed Tribal successor has severe pitch problems in the simulator. Moving a component aft brings only a small improvement, and later adjustments push the pitch figure from 65 to 71 percent. Roll and foreweight offset can improve while pitch remains troublesome. One bridge arrangement hangs over the forward torpedoes, and the design already uses the largest available hull. Ballast offers a real-world way to adjust weight distribution that the simulator struggles to represent.

evidence.note: Pitch readings of 65 and 71 percent, changes in roll and foreweight offset, bridge interference above torpedoes and the comparison with using ballast.

segments.summary: The proposed Tribal successor exposes the limits of moving weapons, changing bridge structures and expanding hull size to correct pitch in the simulator.

segments.title: A destroyer duel against a cruiser-like opponent
segments.body: The game's Russian opponent looks more like a light cruiser, with triple 5.1-inch gun mounts. The destroyer zigzags to make a torpedo firing solution harder to obtain, then combs incoming torpedo tracks while closing the range. Smoke is held until it can make the approach easier. The destroyer loses the duel, but several ships were expected to work together in a flotilla. The expectation that a group would fare better remains a judgment about the scenario, rather than a result demonstrated by this one-on-one trial.

evidence.note: Triple 5.1-inch mounts on the opponent, zigzagging, torpedo combing, delayed smoke use and the criticism of testing a flotilla destroyer alone.

segments.summary: A one-on-one test of the proposed Tribal successor illustrates the difference between fighting alone and operating as part of a flotilla.

segments.title: Soviet destroyer size and small formations
segments.body: One explanation links the size of Soviet destroyers to the number of ships expected to be available for a fight. With fewer ships, the assumption was that they would be more likely to operate singly or in pairs. That in turn favoured more capability on each hull.

evidence.note: Fewer available Soviet destroyers are linked to an expectation of operating alone or in pairs.

segments.summary: The size of Soviet destroyers is linked to an expectation that they would fight alone or in pairs.

segments.title: A destroyer hull with light-cruiser firepower
segments.body: The game allows a destroyer hull to carry several triple turrets and a torpedo launcher. The gun layout and overall firepower make the vessel look closer to a light cruiser. It survives its encounter while the opposing cruiser is lost. The game describes the ship by hull type even when its battery resembles that of a different class of warship.

evidence.note: A destroyer hull carries several triple gun mounts and a torpedo launcher, then survives an engagement in which the opposing cruiser is lost.

segments.summary: A Soviet-style game destroyer carries enough gunfire to invite comparison with a light cruiser, despite its hull classification.

segments.title: An interwar coastal defence ship for Norway
segments.body: The choice begins between a cruiser and a small battleship, then moves to a heavy-cruiser hull in the game's 1925 setting. A compact ship with limited speed and short operating range is the starting point. Heavy guns go forward, with lighter secondary and anti-aircraft weapons. Attempts to control pitch and roll push the hull wider and deeper, making the ship heavier and forcing further adjustments.

evidence.note: Norwegian coastal-defence request, selection of a 1925 heavy-cruiser hull and adjustments to speed, armament and stability.

segments.summary: A simulated 1925 coastal defender for Norway combines heavy forward guns with limited speed and range, then encounters stability and weight problems.
segments.question: What kind of interwar ship could help Norway defend its coast against a German attack?
segments.answerShort: The simulated design uses a 1925 heavy-cruiser hull for a compact coastal defender with heavy guns forward. Stability and weight become the main constraints.

segments.title: Speed, range and period equipment for a coastal defender
segments.body: The early design calls for a compact hull at the lowest practical weight. Coastal service motivates limiting range, and the first speed target is 20 knots. As the hull and machinery change, 24 knots is described as unexpectedly fast for the concept. The build uses radar available in the game, an acknowledged anachronism for the simulated year of 1925.

evidence.note: A 20-knot initial limit, reduced range, a later 24-knot setting and the acknowledged anachronism of using radar in 1925.

segments.summary: The simulated Norwegian coastal defence ship starts with a 20-knot target and limited range.

segments.title: Forward heavy guns and lighter batteries
segments.body: The heavy battery goes forward to make the compact design work. The proposed 6-inch secondaries give way to 5.5-inch guns, treated as a viable period calibre for the role. Three-inch weapons are added for anti-aircraft defence.

evidence.note: Forward main battery, replacement of 6-inch secondaries with 5.5-inch guns and selection of 3-inch anti-aircraft weapons.

segments.summary: A hypothetical Norwegian ship concentrates its heavy guns forward and uses period British calibres for secondary and anti-aircraft duties.

segments.title: Hull width, draught and weight on a coastal defence ship
segments.body: After the gun layout is settled, the design still shows troublesome pitch and roll. More beam helps the game's stability readout at the cost of a heavier hull. Increasing draught puts further pressure on displacement. The design is reported to be 430 tons overweight before more adjustments.

evidence.note: Pitch and roll readings lead to increased beam and draught, followed by a reported 430-ton displacement overrun.

segments.summary: Stability problems on the simulated Norwegian design lead to a wider, deeper hull and a displacement overrun.

segments.title: Armour and torpedoes in the Norwegian design trial
segments.body: The cruiser brings six 9.7-inch guns in the game, with an unusually large torpedo load. The Norwegian design aims to stay outside the cruiser's torpedo reach. Its belt armour absorbs hits while the cruiser suffers damage and fires. Armour and range both influence this particular simulation.

evidence.note: Six 9.7-inch guns and numerous torpedoes on the opposing cruiser, attempts to stay beyond torpedo range and belt armour resisting shell hits.

segments.summary: Keeping a heavy cruiser outside torpedo range lets the Norwegian game design use its belt armour against the opponent's gunfire.

segments.title: The case for a South Korean aircraft carrier
segments.body: A carrier is a plausible option given the importance of South Korea's sea lines of communication. The need to defend them gives the proposal a purpose. The broader strategic case for committing to a carrier remains unsettled.

evidence.note: Sea lines of communication support considering a carrier, while the strategic case receives a tentative assessment.

segments.summary: South Korea's maritime communications give it a reason to consider a carrier.
segments.question: Should South Korea pursue an aircraft carrier?
segments.answerShort: Sea lines of communication give South Korea a reason to consider one. The full strategic case remains open.

segments.title: Compact cruise missiles and shipboard strike capacity
segments.body: The proposal is to carry more compact cruise missiles and make strike capacity more affordable. Related options have been explored, with viability depending on the capability they buy for the price. Railguns and advanced guns offer other approaches to the same cost question. The criticism of the Advanced Gun System centres on poor control of programme scope, with the underlying technology regarded as less of a problem.

evidence.note: Compact cruise missile proposal, cost and capability comparison, and the criticism of AGS programme scope.

segments.summary: Compact cruise missiles would need to offer enough capability for their price; the Advanced Gun System provides a caution about uncontrolled programme scope.
segments.question: Could a compact, low-cost cruise missile increase shipboard strike capacity?
segments.answerShort: Its value depends on capability for the cost. The criticism of the Advanced Gun System concerns control of programme scope.

segments.title: Why France completed Jean Bart
segments.body: Completing Jean Bart gave France a public symbol of recovery. In this interpretation, great-power standing mattered when other naval units also competed for resources. This puts the politics of commissioning the battleship alongside the question of what the fleet needed.

evidence.note: Great-power status and the symbolism of rebuilding France are the stated reasons for completing Jean Bart.

segments.summary: The battleship's completion gave France a visible sign of postwar recovery and great-power standing.
segments.question: Why did France complete Jean Bart when it could have put resources into other warships?
segments.answerShort: The battleship symbolised postwar reconstruction and France's standing as a great power.

segments.title: Larger command ships and uncrewed vessels in European fleets
segments.body: The forecast covers larger European navies as well as smaller ones. Crewed warships could grow as they take on command of groups of uncrewed vessels, which could fill some of the smaller roles and add numbers to the fleet. Even the smaller vessels could reach roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes in this forecast. A radar picket is one example of a ship that could need room for fuel, electronics and backup systems.

evidence.note: Larger crewed command ships, more numerous uncrewed vessels and a projected 2,000-3,000-ton size for demanding uncrewed roles.

segments.summary: A forecast for European fleets combines larger crewed command ships with more numerous uncrewed vessels, including substantial radar pickets.
segments.question: Will smaller European navies end up with fewer, bigger ships or more small ships?
segments.answerShort: The forecast has larger crewed command ships and more numerous uncrewed vessels in some of the smaller roles.

segments.title: Why uncrewed ships need more redundancy
segments.body: A crew can repair a failed system while another unit keeps the ship operating. An uncrewed vessel has to wait for maintenance to reach it, so parallel systems must cover a longer interval without repair. The positioning example assumes two functioning systems are needed to confirm location. A crewed ship carrying three could repair a failed unit while the other two remain active; the suggested allowance for an uncrewed vessel rises to three or four units. These backups add to the hull space required by fuel, machinery and electronics, even for a specialised role such as a radar picket.

evidence.note: Onboard repair versus waiting for visiting maintenance, illustrated by two active positioning systems and additional installed units to cover failures.

segments.summary: Uncrewed ships need installed backups to keep operating until maintenance arrives, increasing the space required for systems such as navigation equipment.

segments.title: Designing a 1930s cruiser for the fictional Albonian Navy
segments.body: The fictional Albonian cruiser is designed to look good on paper and perform poorly in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts. A British-style forward structure and a Japanese-style after structure are combined despite their poor fit, while the armament arrangement takes cues from the German Panzerschiff. A stable model conceals the deliberate absence of deck armour. During the trial, the ship closes the range because its guns are causing little damage, eventually bringing its 3-inch weapons into action. The exercise ends with criticism of split main batteries and the difficulties of controlling their fire.

evidence.note: Deliberately defective Albonian cruiser request, mixed British and Japanese structures, no deck armour, weak gunnery and criticism of a split main battery.

segments.summary: A deliberately flawed Albonian cruiser pairs a stable game model with no deck armour and poor gunnery, exposing weaknesses hidden by its specifications.
segments.question: How would you design a 1930s cruiser for the fictional Albonian Navy that looks good on paper and performs poorly?
segments.answerShort: Combine mismatched structures and a Panzerschiff-style battery on a stable game model, omit deck armour and test the resulting gunnery problems.

segments.title: Mixing British and Japanese components on the Albonian cruiser
segments.body: A British forward section is paired with a Japanese component on the fictional Albonian cruiser. Their fit is awkward in the game designer. The resulting arrangement draws a critical comparison with the Panzerschiff design. The model later shows an engine-efficiency readout of 52.6 percent.

evidence.note: British and Japanese parts, their awkward fit, a Panzerschiff comparison and the 52.6 percent engine-efficiency readout.

segments.summary: British and Japanese components make an awkward combination on the fictional Albonian cruiser.

segments.title: A stable cruiser with no deck armour
segments.body: The ship starts this portion overweight. Stability is deliberately kept respectable so the specification looks credible. The deck has no armour, even with the guns and torpedoes set for the game trial. The favourable stability rating says little about the quality of the protection scheme.

evidence.note: The overweight model retains favourable stability but has no deck armour before entering its trial.

segments.summary: The fictional cruiser has a respectable stability rating while carrying no deck armour.

segments.title: The Albonian cruiser's guns in action
segments.body: The fictional cruiser does little damage at its initial range and moves closer in the simulation. Its 3-inch guns begin firing once the range falls sufficiently. They are judged the most accurate weapons available, with the hope that they will inflict useful damage. Their actual contribution to the result is not established in this exchange.

evidence.note: Closing to 3-inch gun range and hoping that the relatively accurate smaller guns will cause damage.

segments.summary: Closing the range brings the Albonian cruiser's relatively accurate 3-inch guns into action.

segments.title: A split main battery as a fire-control problem
segments.body: Dividing the Panzerschiff's main battery between the forward and after ends of the hull is criticised as a source of fire-control inefficiency. In this interpretation, the arrangement reduces the fighting capability suggested by the guns on paper. The fictional cruiser trial supplies the occasion for challenging favourable accounts of the design. This is a criticism of the layout, without a numerical comparison of real firing performance.

evidence.note: Sarcastic criticism of a main battery divided fore and aft, its fire control and favourable assessments based on paper specifications.

segments.summary: The Panzerschiff's divided main battery attracts criticism for the fire-control problems attributed to its layout.

segments.title: How large might a hypothetical North Korean cruiser be?
segments.body: A small light cruiser provides the rough size benchmark for the imagined North Korean ship. The estimate is off the cuff. Its armour scheme is left open.

evidence.note: A small light cruiser is offered as a rough size comparison.

segments.summary: A small light cruiser is offered as a rough size comparison.
segments.question: What size and armour might a hypothetical North Korean cruiser have?
segments.answerShort: The suggested benchmark is a small light cruiser. The armour is left unspecified.

segments.title: Fitting an A, B and Q turret layout to the G3
segments.body: The requested A, B and Q arrangement can be assembled in the game. A component intended for the G3 fails to fit where expected. Moving it aft makes the arrangement possible, although the resulting position is farther back than desired. The model therefore approximates the proposal within the ship designer's restrictions.

evidence.note: Acceptance of the A, B and Q request, selection of a G3 and a component shifted farther aft to make it fit.

segments.summary: Reproducing the G3's A, B and Q turret arrangement requires compromises with the game's component positions.
segments.question: Can the G3's A, B and Q turret pattern be reproduced in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts?
segments.answerShort: Yes, in approximate form. The game makes some components sit farther aft than intended.

segments.title: Starting a design with maximum survivability
segments.body: The game build begins with maximum survivability and reduces it when the design requires compromises. This is compared with starting a real ship design as a dream specification containing everything wanted. The next step is to work out a cost-effective version.

evidence.note: Maximum survivability reduced as necessary, followed by the analogy between a dream ship and its cost-effective version.

segments.summary: Starting with the desired survivability exposes the compromises needed to reach an affordable ship.

segments.title: Fitting funnels and reducing weight on the G3 model
segments.body: The available funnels will not fit on the original superstructure. Choosing the smallest funnel still leaves a second one to place, so the superstructure has to change. The model then reaches its displacement limit while retaining a speed setting of 33 knots. Pitch and secondary armament still need attention after the weight target is met.

evidence.note: Two small funnels require a superstructure change, followed by weight reduction at a retained speed setting of 33.

segments.summary: Funnel positions force changes to the G3 model's superstructure before weight and pitch can be settled.

segments.title: Why armour substitutes for ballast in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The stock designer has no independent ballast adjustment. Thickening the belt and deck can satisfy its balance calculation, so the resulting armour reflects the simulator's rules as well as the intended protection. The need for unusually thick armour is criticised as a defect in the game's balance model. Another restriction appears when none of the available funnels fit the large secondary tower.

evidence.note: Lack of adjustable ballast, excessive belt and deck armour used to correct balance, and incompatible funnels on the secondary tower.

segments.summary: The G3-inspired model needs unusually thick armour to compensate for the stock game's lack of a ballast adjustment.

segments.title: Gun blast and clear firing arcs
segments.body: The game allows the battlecruiser to fire across its own superstructure. Aboard a real ship, muzzle blast can damage nearby structure. The available firing arc depends on the turret and what lies around it. Even when a turret can train onto a target, the ship's heading may have to change to give the guns clearance.

evidence.note: Firing across the superstructure risks damage, and manoeuvring the ship gives the guns a clear firing direction.

segments.summary: A turret's ability to train towards a target does not guarantee clearance for its muzzle blast.

segments.title: A postwar Tribal-class destroyer in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: An imagined postwar descendant of the Second World War Tribal class is built using the game's 1960 setting. The available large destroyer hull draws an unfavourable comparison with British designs and the Daring class. Several gun sizes compete for a crowded deck, and the design uses oil-fired gas turbines. Altering dimensions and range changes the simulated handling and displacement, with pitch remaining difficult to control. The later trial includes 4.5-inch and 3-inch guns alongside the larger armament and torpedoes.

evidence.note: Request for a postwar Tribal variant, selection of the 1960 game setting, objections to the hull, and attempts to fit weapons while controlling weight and pitch.

segments.summary: A postwar Tribal successor takes shape in the game's 1960 setting, with deck space and persistent pitch constraining its armament.
segments.question: What would a postwar version of the Second World War Tribal-class destroyer look like?
segments.answerShort: The game build uses a large 1960s destroyer hull with mixed-calibre guns and gas turbines. Crowded mount positions, excess weight and persistent pitch constrain the result.

segments.title: Deck space limits the postwar Tribal variant
segments.body: A mount looks too wide for its proposed position, so that location is reserved for another gun. The design also calls for 3-inch weapons and 40 mm guns. Suitable positions for the 40 mm mounts are difficult to find on the selected hull. Deck space is already restricting the armament before the displacement check.

evidence.note: A mount is rejected for its width, followed by the search for positions for 3-inch and 40 mm weapons.

segments.summary: The proposed Tribal successor runs short of suitable positions for its smaller guns.

segments.title: Beam, displacement and pitch on the Tribal variant
segments.body: The simulated destroyer starts well over its weight allowance. The stated speed drops to 36 knots and the design switches to gas turbines. Roll becomes more manageable while the game still reports persistent pitch, including a 65 percent readout during one adjustment. A change to beam improves the pitch estimate and the design goes over its weight limit again.

evidence.note: A 36-knot speed setting, gas turbines, a 65 percent pitch readout and hull changes that reduce pitch but leave the design overweight.

segments.summary: The game designer shows what changing speed, range and hull dimensions does to the destroyer's weight and pitch.

segments.title: What if a German Panzerschiff carried four 14-inch guns?
segments.body: Replacing two triple 11-inch turrets with two twin 14-inch turrets would give a German Panzerschiff larger shells but only four main guns. The low barrel count would slow the establishment of a firing solution. The larger calibre could also alarm other navies and, depending on the timing, undermine acceptance of a 14-inch treaty limit. In that counterfactual, the King George V class could begin with nine 16-inch guns, while Nelson and Rodney receive refits.

evidence.note: Two twin 14-inch turrets attract attention but leave only four guns for establishing a firing solution.
Possible treaty repercussions include nine 16-inch guns for King George V and refits for Nelson and Rodney.

segments.summary: A counterfactual replaces triple 11-inch turrets with twin 14-inch mounts, raising questions about spotting salvos and the naval treaties.
segments.question: How might other navies respond if a German Panzerschiff used twin 14-inch turrets in place of triple 11-inch turrets?
segments.answerShort: The larger calibre would attract attention, although the low barrel count could slow ranging. Depending on the timing, the change might also reopen treaty negotiations and alter British battleship plans.

segments.title: How Project Habakkuk might have changed Cold War carrier strategy
segments.body: The counterfactual turns on whether a pykrete platform could operate across the intended range of latitudes. A large enough runway could bring aircraft such as the SR-71 Blackbird and Avro Vulcan into naval aviation. A fleet of such floating airfields might prevent the conventional supercarrier concept from developing in the same way. Concentrating so much capability in one platform also raises the prospect of an enemy judging a nuclear strike worthwhile against a single ship. Power supply, hull renewal and the number of people needed to crew the platform remain substantial parts of the imagined Cold War design.

evidence.note: Latitude limits, large-aircraft operations, the possibility of nuclear attack and an alternative to conventional supercarriers in the Habakkuk counterfactual.

segments.summary: A successful Habakkuk could make the floating airfield a rival to the conventional supercarrier, with space for aircraft as large as the Vulcan or SR-71.
segments.question: How could a completed Project Habakkuk ice carrier have changed Cold War naval strategy?
segments.answerShort: If a pykrete vessel could operate across latitudes, it might serve as a mobile air base for unusually large aircraft and change how navies invested in carriers.

segments.title: Nuclear electric propulsion for a Habakkuk-scale carrier
segments.body: A nuclear plant could supply enough electricity for the many drives needed to move a Habakkuk-scale carrier. That arrangement suggests an early form of integrated electric propulsion. If it worked, more nations might choose nuclear power for carriers of this kind. Britain is the named example of a navy that could join France in operating a nuclear-powered carrier under this counterfactual.

evidence.note: Nuclear generation supplies multiple electric drives, with Britain identified as a possible additional operator of nuclear-powered carriers.

segments.summary: Nuclear generation could supply Habakkuk's many propulsion drives and bring integrated electric propulsion into the counterfactual earlier.

segments.title: How a floating Habakkuk base might stay in service
segments.body: The imagined long service life depends on continually renewing the pykrete hull while upgrading the equipment it carries. The process of keeping the hull viable would also rebuild it, allowing the platform to remain in service through successive modernisations. Much of that work would have to happen without a conventional dry dock because of the ship's size. An internal dock could launch and recover smaller vessels, while the stores and accommodation could support an entire division of troops. If those assumptions held, a treasury might favour one large initial investment followed by repeated upgrades.

evidence.note: Continual pykrete-hull renewal, upgrades without normal dry-dock access, and an internal dock with stores for a division of troops.

segments.summary: A pykrete carrier's size opens up room for an internal dock while making conventional dry-dock maintenance difficult.

segments.title: Airfield layout and crew demands on Habakkuk
segments.body: A Habakkuk-scale platform could place a large missile installation well away from its airfield. One speculative arrangement puts launchers out at the sides, with missiles turning upwards after launch and room to reload them. Some versions of the imagined platform run to miles in length, giving considerable freedom to separate facilities. Operating such a structure would require a very large crew, even if the extra capacity made it attractive to many navies.

evidence.note: Separated airfield and missile installations, a speculative side-launch arrangement and the large crew required by the proposed scale.

segments.summary: An enlarged Habakkuk might have room to separate aviation and missile facilities at the cost of a much larger crew.

segments.title: Estimating the SCX 26 concept's displacement
segments.body: The proposed SCX 26 is estimated here at roughly 12,000 tonnes if built in steel, above the 8,000-tonne concept figure. The estimate comes from comparing its deck, shape and proportions with the German MEKO A400. A viewer's 16,000-tonne suggestion is considered a possible larger version rather than the preferred estimate. These are judgments about a hypothetical completed ship, with construction material central to the disagreement over displacement.

evidence.note: A steel SCX 26 is estimated at 12,000 tonnes, with the 8,000-tonne figure explicitly disputed.
Deck shape and proportions are compared with MEKO A400, while 16,000 tonnes is considered a possible larger version.

segments.summary: The French SCX 26 is compared with the German MEKO A400 to explain why a steel version might exceed its 8,000-tonne concept figure.

segments.title: A fleet of Habakkuk carriers
segments.body: The counterfactual imagines building four or five Habakkuk carriers and keeping all of them in service into the present. Their assumed longevity would preserve an entire carrier force over many decades.

evidence.note: Four or five Habakkuk carriers are imagined surviving in service into the present.

segments.summary: Four or five long-lived Habakkuk carriers could leave a navy with the same core platforms still in service decades later.

segments.title: Age of Sail parallels for space commerce
segments.body: Regular peacetime convoys seem economically unlikely in this imagined space-trade system. Merchant vessels would operate individually across areas with far fewer patrols and less surveillance than terrestrial seas. International law could still apply, but forces able to enforce it would be scarce. Merchants would therefore need to be self-sufficient and carry weapons for their own protection.

evidence.note: Independent armed merchants are preferred over peacetime convoys in a future with limited patrol and surveillance coverage.

segments.summary: Sparse patrols and the cost of peacetime convoys could favour independent armed merchants in a future space-trade scenario.
segments.question: Would future space travel resemble the Age of Sail, with independent armed merchant ships?
segments.answerShort: Independent armed merchants are plausible in the scenario because routine peacetime convoys would be costly and widely scattered trade would be hard to police.

segments.title: Reloading missile launchers on a Habakkuk-sized ship
segments.body: Moving missiles from storage to launch cells requires space for the weapons and their handling equipment. In the Habakkuk counterfactual, the enormous platform could have a dedicated missile store and a crane reaching over the vertical launch system. That arrangement is proposed as a way to overcome the onboard handling-space constraint on reloading at sea. It is a modern extrapolation from the scale of the historical carrier proposal.

evidence.note: Space for a missile store and a crane over the vertical launch cells is the proposed basis for reloading at sea.

segments.summary: A Habakkuk-sized platform could provide the magazine space and crane access needed to reload vertical launch cells at sea.
segments.question: How might a very large carrier accommodate reloadable missile launchers?
segments.answerShort: Its size could allow a dedicated missile store and a crane that reaches over the vertical launch system to reload the cells at sea.

segments.title: Project Habakkuk alongside the Ford class
segments.body: The smaller Habakkuk length used in this comparison is about 610 metres. The Ford-class comparator is about 337 metres long. On those figures, even the smaller Habakkuk proposal is close to twice the length of the modern carrier. A larger version is considered at up to 1,000 metres.

evidence.note: Stated lengths of 610 metres for Habakkuk and 337 metres for the Ford class, followed by a possible 1,000-metre Habakkuk version.

segments.summary: A 610-metre Habakkuk proposal is compared with a 337-metre Ford-class carrier, before considering a version up to a kilometre long.

segments.title: When steam displaced sail in the Royal Navy
segments.body: Steam offered a way to move when winds and tides would otherwise delay or constrain a ship. The Royal Navy fitted engines before it could count on them for every voyage. A sailing rig remained useful while machinery reliability improved. The 1880s and 1890s are given as the period when ships were consistently built without sailing masts.

evidence.note: Freedom from winds and tides made steam attractive, but unreliable engines prolonged sailing-rig retention into the late nineteenth century.

segments.summary: Engine reliability determined how long ships kept their sailing rigs after the Royal Navy recognised the advantages of steam.
segments.question: When did the Royal Navy recognise that steam would replace sail?
segments.answerShort: The advantage was clear early. It took decades for engines to become reliable enough for ships to dispense with sailing masts consistently.

segments.title: A Japanese answer to the British N3 battleships
segments.body: If Britain builds the N3 class, the counterfactual first has Japan complete its planned Number 13 class, giving it a stronger starting point for subsequent designs. A later move to 20-inch guns remains open.

evidence.note: British N3 construction is linked to Japanese completion of planned capital ships, without settling the later 20-inch-gun question.

segments.summary: A counterfactual about British N3 construction asks whether Japan would have moved to 20-inch guns.
segments.question: Would Japan have pursued a 20-inch-gunned battleship if Britain had built the N3 class?
segments.answerShort: The counterfactual first has Japan complete its planned capital ships, giving it a stronger starting point. A later move to 20-inch guns remains open.

segments.title: Testing Maximus against a Narvik force in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The custom Maximus battleship enters an open-water game trial with friendly destroyers as its screen. The opposing destroyers become separated into groups. To help the group already under attack, the others have to pass the battleship and expose themselves to its guns. Maximus can therefore engage them successively instead of facing a coordinated attack. Near the end, only one enemy destroyer is reported left and no friendly destroyers have been lost. The result belongs to this simulated open-water encounter and its divided enemy force.

evidence.note: Request to test Maximus against a destroyer force based on Narvik.
Separated opposing destroyer groups have to pass the battleship to regroup, while the friendly screen proves difficult to control.
One enemy destroyer remains and no friendly destroyers have been lost in the open-water trial.

segments.summary: Separated enemy destroyer groups let Maximus attack them piecemeal in an open-water game trial inspired by Narvik.
segments.question: Can the Maximus design take on a destroyer force based on Narvik in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts?
segments.answerShort: In the open-water trial, Maximus defeats most of the opposing destroyers piecemeal as they try to regroup. The friendly destroyers are reported intact near the end.

segments.title: Why early boilers took time to adapt to ships
segments.body: Mining and railway boilers supplied early precedents for marine steam. Development on land was still underway as navies considered the technology for ships. Existing designs caused problems at sea that took time to identify and solve. The benefits of steam were apparent before the machinery could be relied on for naval service.

evidence.note: Mining and railway boiler precedents still had problems that had to be understood before they were suitable for ships.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's adoption of steam depended partly on adapting boilers developed for mining and railways.

segments.title: Maximus and the displacement cost of armament
segments.body: The simulated Maximus dispenses with casemate guns and calls for 4.5-inch secondary guns. Its displayed excess displacement reaches about 16,000 tons, and successive reductions still leave it around 13,000 tons overweight. The main battery has twelve guns, with protection and secondary weapons competing for the remaining allowance. The exercise shows the difficulty of completing the desired armament within this particular game's weight calculations.

evidence.note: Casemate removal, a planned 4.5-inch secondary battery and a twelve-gun main battery accompany efforts to reduce a large displayed weight excess.

segments.summary: The simulated Maximus battleship tests how much space and weight the main battery leaves for armour and secondary guns.

segments.title: Maximus and the game's weight budget
segments.body: Superstructure and main-deck protection are reduced while components are moved to recover space and weight allowance. A Littorio-inspired arrangement provides a reference during the revisions. The game does not allow direct adjustment of the ballast calculations, leaving the design dependent on other changes to its fit. It eventually has room for 4.5-inch secondary guns, although additional intended mounts still cannot be placed. The finished model is therefore an approximation of the desired Maximus design within the available controls.

evidence.note: Superstructure and deck-protection reductions, Littorio-inspired layout changes, inaccessible ballast controls and limits on secondary-gun placement.

segments.summary: Reducing protection and rearranging components eventually frees room for Maximus's 4.5-inch secondaries, while the game restricts ballast and mount placement.

segments.title: Controlling destroyer screens in the Narvik game trial
segments.body: The battleship exploits a gap between separated enemy destroyer groups in the simulation. Ships trying to support their companions must pass its guns, so their separation prevents them from concentrating effectively. The friendly screen also has problems: one destroyer collides with the ship it is protecting, while others move away from their expected stations. Separate orders then aim to keep one destroyer close and send another to hunt. The outcome of those revised orders is still open when the trial continues.

evidence.note: Separated enemy groups must pass the battleship to reinforce one another, while friendly screening problems prompt different orders for individual destroyers.

segments.summary: A Narvik-inspired simulation shows how a destroyer screen can lose its position and how separated ships can struggle to regroup.

segments.title: Habakkuk as a floating airfield
segments.body: A proposed kilometre-long carrier could remain off a coastal position and serve as an airfield. On that assumption, most aircraft would have enough runway to take off without the ship moving. Runway length therefore offers a way to operate from a stationary platform in this counterfactual. The proposal depends on constructing a carrier of the enormous scale associated with Habakkuk.

evidence.note: A kilometre-long runway is proposed as sufficient for most aircraft to take off while the carrier remains stationary offshore.

segments.summary: A kilometre-long variant raises the possibility of operating aircraft from a stationary offshore runway.

segments.title: Habakkuk's proposed runway and pykrete construction
segments.body: Habakkuk's possible scale grows from roughly 600 metres to 1,000 metres and then a highly theoretical 1,700-metre design. The largest version would provide a runway longer than a mile, opening the possibility of operating larger aircraft. A projected speed of up to 18 knots would add airflow over that deck. These are proposed dimensions and performance estimates for an unbuilt platform. Successful construction on that scale would also raise questions about what other structures pykrete could support and where they could be built.

evidence.note: Possible 600-, 1,000- and 1,700-metre layouts, an 18-knot projection, and the wider construction possibilities of pykrete.

segments.summary: A highly theoretical 1,700-metre Habakkuk would have a runway longer than a mile, changing the aircraft that a floating base could accommodate.

segments.title: What if HMS Hood had 20-inch guns?
segments.body: Fitting eight 20-inch guns to a Hood-inspired battlecruiser requires a later technology setting in the game. The chosen hull and fittings give the result the appearance of a modernisation. Oil-fired geared turbines provide the propulsion, and reducing cruising range helps bring the design within its weight allowance. Protection against its own enormous main guns is judged an unhelpful design target, although useful armour is still retained. The model comes out at about 50,000 tons with eight 20-inch guns, prompting a separate counterfactual about the effect such a ship would have on naval treaty negotiations.

evidence.note: Later game technology enables the guns, reduced range saves weight, and armour is selected without trying to match the ship's own 20-inch battery.

segments.summary: A game rebuild of Hood shows what changes when eight 20-inch guns drive the choice of hull, armour and cruising range.
segments.question: What would a version of HMS Hood armed with 20-inch guns look like?
segments.answerShort: The game rebuild produces a roughly 50,000-ton battlecruiser with eight 20-inch guns. The battery calls for later technology and compromises on cruising range and armour.

segments.title: Dazzle camouflage and interwar modern art
segments.body: Some modernist art of the 1920s and 1930s was jokingly dismissed as the work of frustrated dazzle-camouflage painters. The imagined painters had no ships left to decorate and turned their designs toward art instead. The anecdote concerns a resemblance between art and naval camouflage, without identifying a particular artist or work.

evidence.note: An interwar joke casts modern art as the work of frustrated dazzle painters who can no longer paint ships.

segments.summary: A joke from the 1920s and 1930s linked modern art to the painters who had once put dazzle patterns on ships.

segments.title: An oversized British battlecruiser at the Washington Naval Conference
segments.body: The counterfactual gives Britain a capital ship with exceptionally large guns and displacement at the time of the Washington negotiations. Other powers are assumed to reject retaining such a powerful ship under anything resembling the historical settlement. British insistence on keeping it would therefore prevent the treaty from taking its familiar form. A replacement agreement and any ships sacrificed to reach it remain unspecified.

evidence.note: Retaining the exceptionally large ship is judged incompatible with a Washington settlement resembling the historical treaty.

segments.summary: An exceptionally large British capital ship would create an obstacle to the Washington settlement if Britain insisted on keeping it.
segments.question: How would a much larger British battlecruiser affect the Washington Naval Treaty if Britain insisted on keeping it?
segments.answerShort: The treaty would be unlikely to follow its historical form. The other powers would have strong reasons to oppose Britain retaining a ship of that size and gun power on the same terms.

segments.title: Superfiring wing turrets in the Orion studies
segments.body: The six-turret arrangement illustrated for the Orion studies aims to outperform contemporary German battleships with the same number of turrets. In the comparison, the British layout puts ten guns on a broadside and eight ahead or astern, against about eight and six respectively for the German layout. Centreline turrets offer the desired broadside with less construction difficulty. Removing the wing turrets also permits a slimmer hull with a greater length-to-beam ratio. Ammunition and hoists become easier to protect because they no longer occupy the exposed wing positions. Fisher favoured wing turrets, although their construction and protection complications weigh against them in this assessment.

evidence.note: British and German gun arcs are compared before the case for centreline turrets turns to construction, hull proportions and ammunition protection.
Fisher's preference for wing turrets.

segments.summary: An Orion-class design study illustrates why the Royal Navy considered superfiring wing turrets and why it settled on a centreline battery.
segments.question: Did the Royal Navy consider battleships with superfiring wing turrets?
segments.answerShort: Yes. The arrangement was considered for the Orion class. Centreline turrets offered the desired broadside with fewer construction and protection complications.

segments.title: Triple turrets for the Orion class
segments.body: The alternative would adapt the 14-inch triple turret Vickers was developing to give Orion five triple 13.5-inch mountings. That arrangement would provide a fifteen-gun broadside and six guns bearing ahead or astern. In the counterfactual, adopting triples so early could lead to Queen Elizabeth-class battleships carrying twelve 15-inch guns, with consequences for their size and displacement. The preference for twin mountings rests on their perceived advantages in operating speed, working space and safety. Concern about the greater complexity of triples helps explain why simply adding barrels was not an automatic choice.

evidence.note: Vickers' developing 14-inch triple turret underpins an Orion alternative, followed by a twelve-gun Queen Elizabeth counterfactual and reasons for retaining twins.

segments.summary: Five triple mountings would give Orion a fifteen-gun broadside, while raising questions about turret complexity and the size of later British battleships.

segments.title: Estimated range of a 20-inch/50 naval gun
segments.body: The rough conventional-range estimate is about 55 to 56 km, with several kilometres of uncertainty. A 16-inch/50 gun provides a comparison at roughly 39 to 40 km. For much of the period under discussion, the larger gun's reach would exceed the ship's ability to acquire a target at that distance, while a slow rate of fire would further limit its usefulness. Using a rounded bore of 500 mm gives a barrel about 25 metres long at 50 calibres. Rocket-assisted ammunition could extend the range, although no figure is given. A further hypothetical use for a barrel this large is launching a cruise missile. Shell weight remains unspecified.

evidence.note: Approximate conventional range, the 16-inch/50 comparison, target-acquisition and firing-rate limits, barrel length, rocket assistance and a hypothetical cruise-missile launch.

segments.summary: A hypothetical 20-inch/50 gun could reach about 55 km, but target acquisition and a slow rate of fire would limit its usefulness.
segments.question: How much range and throw weight might a 20-inch/50 gun provide?
segments.answerShort: The rough conventional-range estimate is about 55 km. Target acquisition and rate of fire would limit its use, and no shell weight is given.

segments.title: The 112,000-ton British battleship limit in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: The battleship is the largest ship type available in this setup, and the selected British hull has a 112,000-ton limit. Comparable limits for other nations are assumed rather than checked. The question uses a historical cutoff of about 1950, with little expected change in battleship options across the remaining game years. The figure describes the game's design allowance.

evidence.note: British battleship hull limit of 112,000 tons and an approximate 1950 cutoff, with other national limits left unverified.

segments.summary: The British battleship selected in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts has a 112,000-ton displacement limit.
segments.question: What is the largest, most heavily armed ship you can build within the game's late-period cutoff?
segments.answerShort: A battleship. The British hull shown has a 112,000-ton limit.

segments.title: Engines and propellant choices on a late-game battleship
segments.body: Poor engine efficiency prompts changes to the game battleship's fuel settings. Its heavy main battery also needs a workable rate of fire. Cordite I is the preferred option for extending range, but it is unavailable for this build. Double-base propellant gives the best range bonus among the available choices, roughly 7.5 percent in the game's statistics.

evidence.note: Poor engine efficiency, concern about heavy-gun firing rate, unavailable Cordite I and a roughly 7.5 percent range bonus from double-base propellant.

segments.summary: Poor engine efficiency and slow heavy guns constrain the game battleship, while propellant choice changes its firing range.

segments.title: Where the weight goes in a 175,000-ton battleship design
segments.body: The game battleship weighs about 175,000 tons against a 112,000-ton hull limit. Engines, boilers, bulkheads, heavy turrets and upper armour account for major entries in the weight breakdown. Reducing the large turrets saves a substantial amount. The original gun count therefore becomes one of the first design choices to change.

evidence.note: The overweight design's machinery, structural protection, turrets and upper armour are reviewed before reducing the battery.

segments.summary: Machinery, bulkheads, turrets and armour push a game battleship to about 175,000 tons against a 112,000-ton limit.

segments.title: Triple versus quadruple turrets on a game battleship
segments.body: Triple turrets retain three-quarters of the original barrels and substantially reduce the battery's weight. The game's rate of fire, base accuracy and aiming speed all improve after the switch. Three guns in a mounting are treated as easier to operate than four. Within this simulation, the smaller battery offers handling advantages as well as a weight saving.

evidence.note: Sixteen barrels become twelve, with lower weight and higher displayed rate of fire, base accuracy and aiming speed.

segments.summary: Replacing quadruple turrets with triples reduces the battery from sixteen guns to twelve while improving the game's firing and aiming statistics.

segments.title: Trading speed and endurance for battleship armour
segments.body: The turret change leaves further cuts to make. Changes to ammunition settings accompany a reduction in range to just under 11,000 on the game's readout and a drop in speed to 30 knots. The redesign leaves about 9,000 tons available for auxiliary machinery and revised armour. The next choices include a 16-inch main belt, a 4-inch inner belt and a 2-inch inner deck.

evidence.note: Range drops to just under 11,000 and speed to 30 knots, leaving about 9,000 tons for auxiliary machinery and protection including a 16-inch belt.

segments.summary: A 30-knot target and shorter operating range get an overweight game battleship under its cap and free weight for protection.

segments.title: How secondary guns affect engagement range in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts
segments.body: In earlier game trials, fitting secondary guns encouraged automated battleships to close until those guns could engage. This design has no secondary battery and continues firing from farther away. Relatively few hits put the opposing battleship in trouble. The aim is to exploit the main battery's reach and inflict damage before the enemy can close effectively.

evidence.note: Past experience with secondary guns drawing battleships closer contrasts with this trial's long-range main-battery engagement.

segments.summary: Omitting secondary guns helps the simulated battleship stay at long range and damage its opponent before closing.

segments.title: How replacing the Pensacolas could change US treaty cruiser design
segments.body: The counterfactual replaces the two Pensacola-class heavy cruisers around their late-1920s commissioning. The US Navy would probably base subsequent treaty cruisers on the substitute design. That would change the starting point for later development. The proposed replacement class cannot be identified confidently from the question.

evidence.note: Replacement of the Pensacolas at commissioning and use of the substitute as a basis for later cruisers, with the replacement class unclear.

segments.summary: Replacing the Pensacolas in the late 1920s could give the US Navy a different starting design for its later treaty cruisers.
segments.question: How might replacing the Pensacola class affect later US Navy treaty cruiser designs?
segments.answerShort: Later treaty cruisers would probably draw on the substitute heavy cruiser design.

segments.title: Would a 152 mm gun make a missile destroyer a cruiser?
segments.body: Turning a missile destroyer into a cruiser would require a more substantial redesign than replacing its main gun. Destroyers and many frigates already carry out cruising and presence missions associated with cruisers. Those shared duties complicate a distinction based solely on ship type or gun calibre.

evidence.note: A larger main gun is insufficient for reclassification, while cruising and presence missions overlap across modern destroyers, frigates and cruisers.

segments.summary: A 152 mm gun alone would not turn a missile destroyer into a cruiser, although destroyers and frigates already perform many cruiser duties.
segments.question: Would fitting a 152 mm gun to a guided-missile destroyer hull make it a cruiser?
segments.answerShort: A cruiser would require a more substantial design change, although many destroyers and frigates already undertake cruiser-like presence missions.

segments.title: How early could warships have carried missiles?
segments.body: The counterfactual begins with missile technology being explored in the early 1930s. It assumes naval planners recognised its potential and committed substantial funding, time and personnel. Under those conditions, some form of shipboard missile capability is considered conceivable by World War II.

evidence.note: Early-1930s experimentation and a speculative World War II capability dependent on foresight and sustained investment.

segments.summary: Early-1930s missile experiments provide the starting point for a speculative wartime shipboard weapon programme.
segments.question: How early could a navy conceivably have converted warships to carry missiles?
segments.answerShort: A programme backed heavily enough in the 1930s might have yielded some form of shipboard capability by World War II.

segments.title: British plans and experiments for warship missile conversions
segments.body: Britain explored missile conversions and carried out experimental work. Relatively few conversions resulted. No particular ship or programme is identified, so the comparison with American practice remains broad.

evidence.note: British conversion work and limited implementation, followed by an unclear final remark about ships that already carried missiles.

segments.summary: Britain explored fitting missiles to existing warships, but relatively few conversions resulted.
segments.question: Did Britain convert existing warships to carry missiles, or draw up plans to do so?
segments.answerShort: Britain explored missile conversions, but relatively few were carried out.

segments.title: Destroyer screening and specialist frigates
segments.body: Anti-submarine warfare is one element of screening a force. A destroyer's screening duties also include air defence. Frigates can specialise in anti-submarine warfare or in other missions. This is a broad distinction by assigned duty, with more complicated cases acknowledged.

evidence.note: Destroyer screening includes anti-submarine warfare and air defence, while frigates can specialise in different duties.

segments.summary: Destroyer screening combines anti-submarine and air-defence tasks, while frigates can concentrate on particular missions.
